transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I guess I’m here because my worrying has gotten hard to put away. Like, once something gets in my head—my mother getting up at night, or a grant report I need to finish, or even whether I missed something at work—I just can’t seem to shelve it, which is funny because I’m a librarian and shelving things is literally part of my life. 

I make lists, and then lists of the lists sometimes, but it doesn’t really quiet down. I try to redirect myself, tell myself it’s handled, but my mind just keeps circling back.
Do these worries ever feel intrusive and unwanted, like they pop into your mind even when you don’t want them to?

Yes, I think so. It’s not like I sit down and decide, “Now I’ll worry about the grant report for the next hour.” It just pops back in, even if I’m shelving books or trying to focus on something else. And then it’s my mother getting up at night, or whether I forgot some tiny work detail… I make lists, which should help, you’d think—librarians and lists, that’s practically a stereotype—but it doesn’t really stay put. I’ll try to redirect myself and it just circles back anyway.
Do you find yourself doing anything over and over—like checking, repeating, or mental rituals—to try to make these thoughts go away or feel less upsetting?

I’m not sure I’d call them rituals, exactly. I do make lists, like I said, and sometimes I’ll look back at them, but… I don’t know if that’s the same thing as checking.

At work, checking is sort of built into the job, you know? Catalog records, call numbers, whether something is in the right collection—there are all these little details, and if one is off, someone notices six months later when they can’t find a thing. We had this one donated set once that was labeled wrong for ages, and—

Sorry, I’m drifting. I guess I don’t really know. I haven’t noticed anything like repeating phrases or doing some set routine to make a thought go away. It’s more that I try to reassure myself I handled it, but the worry doesn’t always listen.
Do you find yourself worrying about many different parts of your life, rather than mainly one specific problem?

Yes, definitely more than one thing. It used to feel mostly centered on my mother—whether she was safe, whether she’d get up in the night and fall, that kind of thing. But over the past year it’s sort of… spread out.

Now it’s finances, or a deadline at work, or whether I made the right call about a staff decision. Even the house—like if something small needs fixing, suddenly I’m imagining it becoming this whole expensive disaster. And then I get into whether I’m being a good daughter, which is hard because there isn’t exactly a checklist for that. I mean, I have checklists for everything else, but not that.

So yes, it’s not one specific problem anymore. It feels like a lot of things can start to seem like they’re about to unravel.
When you start worrying, is it hard for you to stop or control the worry?

Yes. That’s actually a big part of why I came in. Once a worry starts, I can’t seem to… shelve it, I guess, which is a funny thing to say given my job, but that’s what it feels like.

It might be my mother getting up at night, or a grant report, or whether I missed some small work detail. I’ll make a list, check what I can, try to redirect myself to something else, but my mind keeps pulling it back down off the shelf. It doesn’t feel like I’m choosing to keep thinking about it. It just keeps going.
Have you been worrying like this on most days for at least six months?

Yes… most days, I’d say. It’s been about a year and a couple months now, since my mother moved into my home after her fall.

At first I thought it was just adjusting, you know, figuring out where to put her things and how to make the bathroom safer, and then there were all these little practical things—sorry, that’s not really what you asked. But yes, it’s definitely been longer than six months. Around fourteen months, I think.
Do you feel your worrying is out of proportion to what’s actually going on in your life?

Yes… I think so. I mean, some of the things are real—my mother’s safety isn’t imaginary, and money and work deadlines do matter. But the way my mind reacts to them feels bigger than the situation sometimes.

Like a small house repair becomes, in my head, this whole chain of expensive problems, or one staff decision at work turns into me wondering if I’ve messed everything up. It started with worrying about my mother, but now it’s finances, deadlines, the house, whether I’m being a good daughter… it’s like all these different shelves are wobbling at once. So yes, I’d say it’s often out of proportion.
Have you been feeling restless or keyed up?

I’m not sure, actually. “Keyed up” makes me think of someone pacing or unable to sit still, and I don’t know if I’d describe myself that way exactly.

I mean, I do sometimes feel like I should be doing something, but that might just be because there’s always something that needs doing—at work there’s always another request, another cart of materials, someone asking where the microfilm reader is, which nobody seems to remember until it’s urgent. Sorry, that’s not really the point.

I guess I haven’t noticed restlessness specifically. I’d have to think about what you mean by that.
Do you feel these worries are mainly a reaction to your mother moving in after her fall?

I think it started that way, yes. When my mother moved in after the fall, everything felt like it was about keeping her safe—making sure she wouldn’t slip, whether I was home enough, whether I’d miss something important.

But it hasn’t stayed just there. It’s sort of… spread. Now I’ll worry about money, or a staff decision at work, or a deadline, or something in the house that needs fixing. Even a small thing can start to feel like it’s about to unravel into ten other things.

And then I get stuck wondering if I’m being a good daughter, which loops back to my mother again. So it’s connected, I suppose, but it’s not only about her anymore.
Have you been having muscle tension?

Yes, I think so. By the end of the day my neck and shoulders feel… almost locked, like I’ve been holding them up around my ears without noticing.

And I catch myself clenching my jaw a lot—usually when I’m answering emails, or if I’m trying to listen for my mother in the next room. Which sounds a little silly, because she might just be watching television or moving a chair, but I’ll realize my teeth are pressed together and my shoulders are tight. So yes, there’s definitely tension there.
Since your mother moved in, have there been times when your worrying was only about that situation, rather than about lots of different things?

At first, yes, it felt like it was just about my mother and whether she was safe after she moved in. Like, was the rug going to catch her foot, did I hear her moving around, should I have arranged the furniture differently—things like that.

But over this past year it hasn’t really stayed contained there. It’s spread into money, things at work like staff decisions or deadlines, and then stuff around the house. Even something small can start feeling like it’s going to unravel into a whole chain of problems.

And then somehow it circles back to whether I’m being a good daughter anyway, so… I guess there were times early on when it was mostly about her, but now it’s about lots of different things.
Have you been having trouble sleeping?

Yes… I have. Most nights I get into bed and then my mind just keeps going. I’ll replay what happened that day, then start planning for everything that could go wrong tomorrow—work things, the house, my mother.

And if I wake up because I hear her moving around, even if it’s probably nothing, I’m just… awake after that. Sometimes for an hour or two. I’ll lie there listening, thinking whether I should get up, whether I missed something.

Then I go into the library the next morning feeling like I slept, technically, but didn’t really rest.
Has this worrying been interfering with your daily life?

Yes… it has. I mean, I still go to work and do what I’m supposed to do, but I’ve started missing small things at the library—details I normally would catch right away. And in our line of work, small details matter, you know, catalog notes, schedules, who’s covering what… it’s not glamorous, but it’s how everything keeps moving.

There was also a grant presentation recently where I just sort of froze. I had to hand off parts of it to someone else, which was embarrassing. I kept thinking afterward about how I used to be the person people relied on in those moments.

So yes, it’s interfering. Mostly it’s made me worry whether I’m still leading my team well, which is… hard to admit.
